title: Chapter 46: Rowan Writes Back, Part 4 of 5: Rowan
html:
He came up through the hole in the floor the way you come up out of water. Head and shoulders first, quickly, looking round. Then the rest of him, in one movement, onto the boards, and up onto his feet, and back against the wall by the ladder, all before she had taken a breath.
And then he stood there.
And she stood there.
And between them, in the middle of the little square room, the great black iron clock stood with its wheels not turning and its weights hanging down at the ends of their chains, and the gray feathers from the pigeons came down slowly through the green light from the round window, turning, and settled on the dusty boards.
He was tall.
That was the first thing. She had known it. Juno had said it. Wren had said it, in the Ledger. Sixteen, tall for his age. But knowing it was not the same. The last time she had stood in a room with him, he had come up to her shoulder. Now she would have had to tip her head back to look him in the eyes. He was taller than she was by a hand. He was nearly as tall as their father had been.
And thin. So thin. The gray cadet's coat with its high stiff collar hung off his shoulders the way the doctor's coat hung off the doctor, and his wrists stuck out of the sleeves, long and bony, with the knuckles of both hands scraped raw. His dark hair was cut so short that she could see the shape of his skull under it. His face had changed shape. It had been round, and soft, and always a little dirty. Now it was long, and narrow, and pale, and the bones of the cheeks stood out under the skin, and the mouth was a straight line.
It was their father's face. Not now. Not the gray face in the hay that tapped and did not speak. The face from before. From the portrait at the top of the stairs at Crown Walk. The young Lord Thorne in his first coat of office, painted at twenty, looking out of the frame with his chin up as if he expected somebody to argue with him.
Only the eyes were not their father's.
The eyes were dark, and straight, and steady. And they were looking at her the way you look at a room you have been afraid to go back into for a very long time, to see what is still there.
She knew those eyes. She saw them every morning, in the bottom of a tin basin, when she washed her face.
He looked at her hair.
She saw him look at it. The cropped dark ends sticking out under Ellis's cap. His eyes went to it and stayed there for a moment, and something moved in the straight line of his mouth.
"You cut it," he said.
His voice had broken. She had known that too. She had not known what it would sound like. It was low, and a little rough, and careful, like the voice of somebody who has been told many times to speak up and speak clearly and has learned to do it without ever once raising it.
"I sold it," said Lyra.
He did not say anything to that.
He looked away from her, round the room. At the clock. At the hole in the ceiling with the bell hanging dark above it. At the round green window. At the ladder in the corner and the square hole in the floor beside him, where he had come up. He looked at everything, quickly, the way the cadets were taught to look, from left to right and back. Corners. Doors. Shadows.
"The big man," he said. "In the crypt door. At the bottom."
Lyra's heart turned over.
"I told him not to come up."
"I know. He didn't." Rowan's eyes came back to her. "I saw him from the path. Standing in the door with his arms folded. He didn't move when I went past. He looked at me, and didn't move." He paused. "It's Oren, isn't it."
"Yes."
"In somebody else's coat. Too short in the arms."
"Yes."
Rowan looked at the floor for a moment.
"He taught me to ride," he said. "On the gray pony. In the park. He used to walk beside me with his hand on the saddle, the whole way round, so I wouldn't fall off. And then one day he took his hand off and didn't tell me, and I went all the way round on my own, and when I got back he was standing at the gate, and I said you let go, and he said you didn't need it." He looked up. "He didn't look at me like that, today. Like he knew me. He looked at me like he was deciding whether to kill me."
"He wouldn't."
"No." Rowan's mouth moved. "I don't suppose he would."
He did not come away from the wall.
He stood there with his back to the stone and his scraped hands at his sides, and she stood by the stopped clock with the little gray paper crushed in her fist, and the space between them was perhaps four steps. Five. Across the dusty boards, past the iron frame. She could have crossed it. She did not. She had the feeling, very strong, that if she took one step toward him he would go back down the ladder, and she would never see him again.
"I said I was going to the chophouse," said Rowan. "To take the plate back. The Inquisitor sends my dinner from the chophouse on Chancery Lane, every day, on a plate. I said I'd take it back myself. The sergeant doesn't count us again till the fourth bell." He looked at the little brass dial by the window. At the two brass hands. "That's not right, that clock."
"No. It stopped. A long time ago."
"I know." He looked at it a moment longer. "She said it was a fine thing. A place where it's always the same time."
Lyra could not speak.
"You remember," she said at last. It came out as a whisper. "You remember that."
"I remember everything." He said it flatly. Not proudly. The way you say I have a cough. "I've never burned anything. Not one stone. The Academy gives you skills, bought, little stones from the Bank, so you know how to fight and ride and shoot without learning. They go in here." He touched the side of his head, behind the ear. "But you don't have to burn anything to use them. They're not yours, so they don't cost you. So I've never spent anything of mine." He looked at her. "I remember every room in Crown Walk. I remember the smell of the stairs. I remember the day they came for Father, and you weren't there."
The green light wavered on the boards.
"I remember standing in the hall," said Rowan, "with the men in gray going past me up the stairs. And Aunt Cressida holding my shoulder. And her saying, Your sister has done this, darling. Your sister has brought this on us all." He did not move. "And I remember that you weren't there to say she was wrong."
Lyra opened her mouth.
"Don't," said Rowan. "Not yet. I'm not finished." His voice did not rise. It was very steady. Too steady. Like a boy reciting a lesson he has learned by heart and said to himself in the dark a thousand times. "And then I went to the Academy. And everybody knew the name. And they looked at me. And I didn't know where to sit. And a man came out of a room at the end of a long office and gave me a barley sugar and showed me how to fold the wrapper. Small. So my face would keep still." He swallowed. "And he's been kind to me every day since. Every single day. For two years. And you sent me letters every month that I didn't open, and then you stopped, and then you were gone, and they said you'd stolen Father out of a hospital and run away down the river with a harvester who'd killed a man."
He stopped.
"That's what I know," he said. "That's everything I know. Now you tell me what you know. And then I'll ask my question."
He folded his arms.
The pigeons had come back. Lyra heard them, very softly, muttering up in the dark under the beams, above the bell.
She uncurled her fist, and looked at the little gray paper in her palm, creased into a hundred tiny diamonds, with his five lines on it and the R with its little sword.
Then she put it back inside her coat. And took a breath. And told him.
Everything
She had thought she would start at the beginning. She had planned it, on the hundred and four steps. The day the men in gray came. Where she had been. Why.
She did not start there.
She started with their father's hand.
"He taps," she said.
Rowan did not move.
"Father. He taps. With one finger. On anything. The wall, the blanket, the side of the bed. On your hand, if you give it to him." She held up her own right hand, and tapped her first finger against her thumb, slowly, so he could see. "Four. Then two. Then nine. Then three. And then he stops, and waits. And then he does it again. Over and over. He's been doing it for two years, Ro. Since the beginning. Since before they took him to Fallowfield. The nurses wrote it down in his notes. Patient taps. As if it was a cough. As if it was nothing."
She put her hand down.
"It isn't nothing. It's a drum call. From the war. From the Commonwealth Foot. Four is witness. Two is hold. Nine is fold. Three is home." She heard her own voice, very steady, the way his had been steady. "There's a sergeant who knows the calls. A Watch sergeant. He came out to where we had Father hidden, on Monday, and he tapped back. On Father's hand. And Father answered him."
Rowan's arms were still folded. But his face had changed. Not much. A little. The straight line of the mouth had gone a little less straight.
"Answered," he said.
"He tapped once. The answer. It means heard." Lyra's throat went tight. She made it open. "And then he looked at the sergeant. Properly. With his eyes. Like a person. And he said something. Out loud. Drum. Drummer. The drummer. Find—" She stopped. "And then he stopped. And went back to tapping."
The green light wavered on the boards.
"He's in there, Ro," she said. "He's not empty. They told us he was empty. A Slate. Gone. They told us it was kinder to put him somewhere quiet and let him forget. And he's not gone. He's been in there for two years, tapping the same thing, over and over, because it's the only thing he's got left to tell anybody with, and nobody was listening."
Rowan said nothing.
She told him the rest.
She told him about the hospital at Fallowfield, and the night she and a man with a book had taken Father out of it, and why. She told him about the barge. About a woman called Hessa with a black barge and a baby called Robin and a husband with a bad shoulder, who had hidden their father in the hay for a week and not taken a penny. About the locks, and the hooks, and the ice. About Juno, who was fourteen and had walked fourteen miles on frostbitten feet to bring her a catalogue.
She told him about the catalogue.
"The Memory Bourse," she said. "On Lantern Quay. The Lady Vivienne's house. On Midwinter they sell things. Not paintings. Not jewels. People. What's in people. Childhoods. Loves. A war." She swallowed. "And Lot Forty-one is called A Lord's Last Evening. Taken whole, before the fire."
Rowan's arms came unfolded.
Not all the way. Only a little. His hands came down from his chest, slowly, and stopped at his sides.
"Father's," he said.
"Father's. The last evening before he started tapping. Taken out of him whole, the night everything went wrong, by a harvester. And put in a jar. And sealed. And kept in the cold, under the Lady's house, for two years." Lyra looked at him. "And now somebody's selling it. To the highest bidder. Sealed bids. At midnight on Midwinter."
"Who?"
"It says in the catalogue. Under the lot. C. T., by proxy."
Rowan stood very still.
She watched him hear it. She watched the letters go into him, the way they had gone into her, on the barge, by Hessa's lamp, a week ago, when Juno brought the catalogue. C. T. She watched him see them. Small. In a corner. At the bottom of a letter. In purple ink, on thick cream paper, smelling of lilies. The way they had both seen them, a hundred times, since they were small, on the cards that came with the birthday presents and the Midwinter presents and the notes that said Darling, your aunt is coming to tea.
"No," said Rowan.
"Yes."
"No. She—" He stopped. "She took me in. When you were gone. She held my shoulder in the hall. She paid for the Academy. She comes to the visitors' day every month, and brings a cake." His voice had gone strange. Not louder. Thinner. "She cried at Father's bed. At Fallowfield. I saw her. She held his hand and cried."
"Did he tap?"
Rowan looked at her.
"When she held his hand," said Lyra. "When she cried. Did he tap on her?"
Rowan did not answer for a long moment.
"No," he said at last. Very quietly. "No. He took his hand away."
The pigeons muttered above the bell.
"I didn't know it was her," said Lyra. "Not at first. Not for certain. I didn't want to know. When I saw C. T. in the catalogue, I told everybody I didn't know who it was. I lied. To the people who were keeping me alive. For a week." She looked at the floor. "I've stopped lying now. It was too heavy."
She looked up.
"I didn't do it, Ro. Whatever she told you in the hall. I didn't bring it on us. I wasn't there when they came, and I've been sorry every single day for two years that I wasn't there. But I didn't do it." She held his eyes. "I don't know all of who did. I know some of it. I know her name's on the jar. I know an old harvester with blue fingers carried it to the Lady's door, and asked for no money, and said to keep it cold." She paused. "And I know that the night before they came for Father, you and I were sent to bed early, and the house was full of men's voices in the study till very late. And one of them was hers."
Rowan's hand went to his chest.
She saw it go. The way Wren had seen it go, though Lyra did not know that. Flat. Over the place under his coat where a year-old letter lay against his skin, cream paper, crumpled, with another boy's blood on it.
"That's what I know," said Lyra. "That's everything. Except where I am, and who I'm with, and what we're going to do. I won't tell you those. Not because I don't trust you." She stopped. "Yes. Because I don't trust you. Because you walk up the Ministry Steps every morning and sit on a bench outside his door and eat his pie. And I don't know yet what you'd do, if he asked you kindly."
Rowan did not flinch.
"No," he said. "Neither do I."
They stood there, the two of them, on either side of the stopped clock. Four steps apart. Five.
And then Rowan Thorne took his hand away from his chest, and looked at it, as if it were somebody else's.
"That's not my question," he said.
How Do You Know?
He did not ask it at once.
He stood by the wall and looked at the stopped clock for a long time. At the great black iron frame, and the wheels inside it with their teeth like saws, and the long arm going up through the wall, and the two iron weights hanging at the ends of their chains in the dark slot in the floor, where they had come down and stopped a hundred years ago.
Then he looked at the little brass dial by the green window. Twenty past four.
"The Inquisitor says," said Rowan, "that a Slate is like a clock."
Lyra did not move.
"He said it on my first week. In his room. I asked him about Father. I asked him if Father knew I was there, when I went to Fallowfield. If he could hear me." Rowan's voice was very even. "And the Inquisitor was kind about it. He's always kind. He took off his spectacles and he said: Rowan, a man who has been emptied is like a clock that has been wound and then left. The wheels go on turning, for a while. The hands go round. It looks like time. It sounds like time. But nobody is reading it. Nobody is there." Rowan looked at the dial. "And then one day the weights reach the bottom, and it stops. And you will find that you are glad."
The pigeons had gone quiet again.
"And I believed him," said Rowan. "Because he was kind, and because it made it easier. And I stopped going to Fallowfield. After the third time. Because the tapping made me feel sick, and the Inquisitor said it was only the wheels going round."
He turned his head and looked at her.
And she saw that the straight line of his mouth had gone. It was a boy's mouth again. Sixteen. Shaking at the corner.
"So that's my question," he said. "How do you know?"
Lyra looked at him.
"How do you know it isn't just the wheels?" said Rowan. "How do you know it's him? How do you know it means anything? You say a sergeant tapped back and Father answered. You say he looked at somebody with his eyes. You say he said drummer. How do you know that wasn't just—a wheel catching? A tooth slipping on a cog? How do you know there's anybody in there reading it?" His voice did not rise. It went thinner, and thinner, like a thread pulled too tight. "Because if you're wrong, Lyra, if it's only the wheels, then I've been right to stay away. And if you're right—"
He stopped.
"If you're right," he said, "then I left him. For two years. Tapping. With nobody."
The green light wavered.
Lyra did not answer with words.
She crossed the room.
Four steps. Five. Past the iron frame of the clock, across the dusty boards, through the slow gray falling of a feather. He saw her coming and his body went stiff against the wall, the way Wick's had gone stiff on his sack, and for one moment she thought he would go down the ladder.
He did not.
She stopped in front of him. Close. And held out her right hand, palm up, between them.
"Give me your hand," she said.
Rowan looked at her hand.
He looked at it for a long time. Her hand. Red with cold, and rough, with the skin split across the knuckles, and ink in the cracks, and the nails broken short. Not a lady's hand at all. Not any more.
Then, slowly, as if from very far away, he unfolded his scraped right hand from his side, and laid it on hers. Palm down.
It was cold. Colder than hers. Long and thin and bony. Their father's hand. She held it.
And with the first finger of her other hand, on the back of his, she tapped.
Four.
The way Father tapped. Not hard. Not quick. Each tap separate and clear, like a drop of water falling into a bucket in a quiet room. Lifting, and falling. On the bones of the back of his hand, between the scraped knuckles.
Two.
Nine.
Three.
And then she stopped. And held his hand. And waited. The way Father waited.
Rowan did not move.
He stood against the wall with his hand lying in hers and looked down at it, at her finger resting now on the back of his, still. And she watched his face. And she saw it change. Not soften. Change. Go white, the way paper is white, the way Juno said it had gone at the pump, the way Wren had seen it go in the Long Office, though Lyra did not know that. His eyes went wide. And then they went somewhere else. Not to her. Not to the clock. Somewhere far away, and a long time ago, and very near.
"He does that," said Rowan.
His voice was hardly a voice at all.
"Who?" said Lyra. "Father. Yes. That's what I'm—"
"No." Rowan's eyes came back to her. Wide. Black. "No. Not Father. The Inquisitor."
The tower was very quiet.
"He taps that," said Rowan. "On his desk. When he's reading. With one finger. On the green leather. Four, and two, and nine, and three. And then he stops, as if he's waiting for something. And then he goes on reading." His hand in hers had begun to shake. "Every day. For two years. I sit on the bench outside his door and I can see him through the gap, and he taps it. I thought it was a habit. Like the wrappers. I thought it was what his hands did when he was thinking." He swallowed. "I tap it. Sometimes. In bed. With the lamp out. I didn't know I'd learned it. I didn't know what it was. I thought I'd got it from him."
Lyra did not let go of his hand.
She stood very still, in the cold, in the green light, by the stopped clock, holding her brother's hand. And she felt it go into her, what he had said. Slowly. Like the cold going in through the soles of her boots in the graveyard. All the way up.
She had known he knew it. Moll had seen him tap it once, on Monday, over his papers, and Oren had brought that into the city too. She had thought it was a trap. A thing laid down for one man, to see if he would step in it. But this was not once. This was every day. For two years. Since the very winter that Father began.
The man who folded papers small. The man who had given her brother a barley sugar on his first day and taught him how to keep his face still. The man who had said a Slate was like a clock that nobody was reading. He sat at his green leather desk, every day, for two years, and tapped her father's drum call with one finger, and waited.
Waited for what?
For somebody to answer.
"That's how," she said.
Rowan looked at her.
"That's how I know," said Lyra. Her voice was shaking now too. She let it. "Because it isn't a wheel, Ro. A wheel doesn't go on turning in two men. A wheel doesn't jump from our father's hand to an Inquisitor's desk to a Watch sergeant's table to a boy's bed in the Academy with the lamp out. That's not a clock. That's a message." She held his hand harder. "It's a message, and it's been going round and round this city for twenty years, from hand to hand, and everybody who knows it is either trying to answer it, or trying to stop anybody else from hearing it. And Father's been sending it for two years. From inside. Because he's still there. Because there's somebody there to send it."
She stopped. She breathed.
"And you didn't leave him, Ro," she said. "You were told he was gone, by a man who knew he wasn't. That's not leaving. That's being lied to."
Rowan stood against the wall with his hand in hers and his face white and his eyes wide.
"There's an answer," said Lyra. "To the call. When you hear it, and you know someone's sending it, you answer. Once. Just once. It means heard." She looked at him. "That's all. That's all Father's been waiting for. For two years. Somebody to tap once."
She let go of his hand.
She did not take hers away. She left it there, palm up, between them, with his lying on top of it. So that he could take his away if he wanted. So that it was his choice.
Rowan looked down at their two hands.
He did not take his away.
And after a long, long moment, in the cold, in the green light from the round window, under the great dark bell, beside the clock that had said twenty past four for a hundred years, his long first finger lifted from the back of her hand.
And fell.
Once.
